title: Architecture that makes changes easier
subtitle: Use MVC, MVVM, dependency injection, and repositories to give each responsibility a clear owner.
objectives: Recognize when a view controller has accumulated unrelated responsibilities.
Separate transport models, domain rules, presentation state, and UIKit rendering.
Inject replaceable dependencies through small protocols.
Keep one authoritative owner for shared task data.
Use coordinators where navigation complexity justifies them.
prerequisites: Days 10–12: async services, screen state, cancellation, and rendering.
Protocols, initializers, value types, and ARC.

sections.title: 1. Start with responsibilities, not folder names
body: MVC remains a useful UIKit model: models represent application data and rules, views display content and accept input, and controllers connect them. Problems arise when the controller also constructs HTTP requests, decodes JSON, manages a database, formats every field, and coordinates several navigation flows. The issue is the number of responsibilities, not the fact that a class ends with ViewController.

Architecture should make a likely change local and testable. Ask where a new API field, a business validation rule, or a different presentation belongs. Moving a thousand-line controller into a thousand-line view model does not solve unclear ownership. Split along meaningful boundaries and keep small features simple until there is a demonstrated need for another abstraction.

sections.title: 2. MVVM separates presentation decisions from widgets
body: A view model owns UI-facing state and transforms domain values into display values. A controller creates and configures UIKit objects, forwards user actions, and renders state. The view model should not need a UILabel or UINavigationController to decide that a completed task has a Completed subtitle. That lets tests evaluate behavior without constructing a window.

For a UIKit application, marking the view model @MainActor is often a clear choice because its state is observed by the UI. It can await a repository without blocking network waits. Decide whether the view model owns unstructured task handles or exposes async methods whose caller owns the task; both can work, but mixing the policies unpredictably makes cancellation and lifetime harder to reason about.

sections.title: 3. A repository is a data policy boundary
body: An API client speaks HTTP. A persistence store speaks files or database operations. A repository exposes domain operations such as listTasks or toggleTask and decides where authoritative data comes from. An offline-first repository might read local records immediately, synchronize remote changes, and publish accepted updates. A small in-memory repository is excellent for learning and deterministic tests.

Do not maintain separate writable task arrays in the inbox, board, and detail controller with no synchronization rule. Let a repository or shared domain store own task values, and let screens own presentation state such as selected filters. A screen may hold a snapshot for rendering, but mutations should flow through the authoritative owner so other screens can refresh or observe changes consistently.

sections.title: 4. Dependency injection makes choices explicit
body: Constructor injection gives a type the services it needs when it is created. A protocol describes the smallest useful capability, such as fetchTasks, rather than duplicating every method of a concrete class. A composition root near app or scene setup chooses production implementations and connects the graph. Tests choose a fake without changing the view model.

Protocols are not mandatory for every struct. They are valuable at changeable or nondeterministic boundaries: network, storage, time, authentication, and navigation. Avoid service locators and shared singletons as a shortcut for every dependency; they hide requirements and make tests depend on global state. Also avoid dozens of one-line layers that simply forward a call without clarifying a responsibility.

sections.title: 5. Navigation and ownership belong in the design
body: A coordinator can own a navigation flow and construct its screens, keeping route decisions outside presentation logic. The coordinator typically owns the navigation controller and any active child coordinators; a screen signals intent through a delegate or closure. Ensure these references do not form a retain cycle. A parent must retain a coordinator for as long as its flow is active.

For a single simple push, a controller can navigate directly. Introduce a coordinator when routes, authentication gates, deep links, or multi-step flows become difficult to maintain. Folder organization can group code by feature, with shared infrastructure separate, but folder structure is only a map. Review actual dependency direction: business rules should not import your entire UI layer just to validate a task title.

example.title: A repository-backed, UIKit-independent view model
walkthrough: This Foundation-only file demonstrates the architecture boundary; it deliberately contains no UIKit widgets. Add it to an app or suitable Swift target and await demonstrateArchitecture() from an async context.
TaskRepository is Sendable so its implementation can cross from the main-actor view model to an actor-backed store safely. The actor serializes mutations to its task array.

TaskRecord represents domain data. TaskRow represents one screen's display values. They need not remain separate in every tiny app, but the distinction becomes useful when formatting and server contracts evolve.

The view model exposes an async reload method. In a controller, store the Task handle that calls it and cancel according to the screen's lifecycle; do not create an untracked load on every appearance.
The composition root decides the concrete repository. Replacing MemoryTaskRepository with a tested remote/local implementation does not require rewriting the renderer.
example.expectedOutput: The demonstration prints ["To do", "Completed"]. A controller can render the same state without knowing whether the records came from memory, HTTP, or persistent storage.

exercises.title: Move presentation logic out of a cell
exercises.prompt: A custom cell formats a task's status in several conditionals. Create a pure presentation value with a title, status text, and accessibility summary.
requirements: Keep UIKit out of the presentation type.
Make complete and incomplete behavior explicit.
hints: A value type can calculate display properties during initialization.
Keep styling in UIKit while returning meaningful text.
exercises.explanation: The cell now applies values instead of deciding domain meaning. These strings are English for the exercise; production localization should use localized resources and appropriate formatting. Do not set an accessibility label blindly if it would duplicate text already read from accessible subviews.
checks: A completed task maps to Completed and an incomplete task to To do.
The UUID matches the original task.
The type can be tested without importing UIKit.

exercises.title: Inject a repository that fails predictably
exercises.prompt: Build a fake repository that throws a known error. Use it to verify that TasksViewModel reaches its recoverable failure state.
requirements: Conform to TaskRepository without a network call.
Do not depend on a real server being offline.
hints: A stateless struct can safely conform to Sendable.
A dedicated test error keeps the failure deterministic.
exercises.explanation: This fake represents a specific boundary outcome and makes the test repeatable. It verifies behavior that matters to the user: the view model offers a recoverable failure state. Day 16 converts this kind of check into XCTest assertions and adds success, empty, and cancellation coverage.
checks: The verification returns true every time without internet access.
Changing the fake to return an empty array leads to ready with zero rows.
Explain why a real timeout would be a slower and less reliable unit test.

exercises.title: Extract a navigation flow
exercises.prompt: Create a small coordinator that owns a navigation controller and pushes a task detail controller when a list emits a task-selection closure.
requirements: Use a weak coordinator capture in the selection closure.
Retain the coordinator from the scene or another owner.
Pass the selected task ID to the detail screen.
Keep this routing choice out of the view model.
hints: The coordinator can create the list in start().
The scene must keep a strong property for the coordinator.
exercises.explanation: The two screen classes are routing placeholders; connect onSelect to the actual list delegate and build the detail UI separately. Retain TasksCoordinator as a scene property, create it with the scene's navigation controller, and call start. The navigation controller retains its screens, so their callbacks should not strongly retain the coordinator that owns it.
checks: Trigger onSelect with a UUID and inspect that same UUID in the detail screen.
Pop the detail controller and confirm it can be released.
Remove the scene's coordinator reference during teardown and inspect the ownership graph.

quiz.question: What is the main value of dependency injection?
options: It requires every type to become a protocol
It makes dependencies explicit and replaceable
It guarantees no bugs
It removes the need for initializers
quiz.explanation: Injection reveals a type's requirements and lets a composition root or test supply suitable implementations.

quiz.question: Which operation best belongs in an API client?
options: Choosing a label's font
Building and validating an HTTP request
Pushing a detail controller
Deciding row spacing
quiz.explanation: An API client translates between the app and an HTTP contract. Rendering and navigation have different responsibilities.

quiz.question: Where should a task's authoritative completion value live?
options: Independently in every cell
In a shared domain store or repository with an explicit policy
Only in a navigation controller
In a screenshot of the row
quiz.explanation: Screens may render snapshots, but mutations need an authoritative owner so the inbox, board, and detail screen do not diverge.

quiz.question: Does moving all controller code into a view model automatically produce good MVVM?
options: Yes, class naming is the entire architecture
No, responsibilities and dependency direction still matter
Yes, if the file is longer
Only if it imports every framework
quiz.explanation: A large view model can still mix networking, persistence, presentation, and routing. Separation should follow responsibilities rather than labels.

quiz.question: Who should usually choose concrete repository implementations?
options: Every reusable cell
The composition root near app or scene setup
The JSON decoder
A hidden global lookup in every method
quiz.explanation: A composition root assembles the dependency graph once and makes environment choices visible and reviewable.

pitfalls: Moving a massive controller unchanged into a massive view model.
Keeping multiple independently writable copies of domain state.
Using global singletons to conceal dependencies.
Adding protocols and forwarding layers without a real change or test boundary.
Letting a coordinator be released immediately after start.
Creating strong cycles through coordinator-owned screens and callbacks.
checkpoint: Draw the dependency direction from UIKit to view model to repository.
Replace the real repository with a deterministic fake.
Explain who owns task data versus screen filter state.
Show where request handles are owned and cancelled.
Justify each architectural layer by a concrete responsibility or likely change.

capstone.title: PocketTasks milestone: a maintainable feature boundary
steps: Keep the inbox controller focused on UIKit construction, binding, and rendering.
Inject a task repository into the view model and provide memory and remote implementations.
Choose one task-data authority for inbox, board, and details.
Write a short dependency diagram and explain whether a coordinator is needed for your current flow.
